statement: Ten 2s are multiplied together: $2 \times 2 \times 2 \times \dots \times 2$. What is the last digit of the answer?

choices.misconception: I added the ten 2s instead of multiplying them, got 20, and took its last digit.
I miscounted along the pattern and found the last digit for nine 2s instead of ten.
I saw the pattern 2, 4, 8, 6 and stopped after two full rounds, forgetting the last two 2s.
I counted the first 2 as step zero of the pattern, so I went one step too far.

hints: Find the last digit for one 2, then two 2s, then three 2s.
Try small cases. Only the last digit matters each time you multiply by 2 again, so look for a pattern in the last digits and see where the tenth one falls.
The last digits go 2, 4, 8, 6, then 2, 4, 8, 6 again, then 2, 4. The tenth is 4. Indeed, ten 2s multiply to 1024.

solutions.reliable: Small cases: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, ... The last digits go 2, 4, 8, 6 and then repeat. Two full rounds use eight 2s and end on 6; the ninth 2 gives 2 and the tenth gives 4. Check by multiplying: ten 2s make 1024, which ends in 4. The transferable idea: when a calculation is long, work out the first few cases and let the pattern carry you the rest of the way.
solutions.elegant: Five 2s make 32, which ends in 2, and 2 x 2 ends in 4. So ten 2s, which is 32 x 32, ends in the same digit as 2 x 2: 4.

whyOnTest: Nobody expects you to multiply ten 2s fast; trying one, two, three 2s reveals a short repeating pattern, the habit this checks.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
